tagline: Two desert roads follow the Green River and its reservoir
intro: The Flaming Gorge–Green River Basin Scenic Byway follows roads on both sides of the reservoir through high desert and red rock country. Wyoming’s Transportation Commission adopted it into the state scenic byways program, and the Wyoming Office of Tourism presents the reservoir and its rock formations as the drive’s attractions. The tourism office gives the 100-mile byway a minimum driving time of three hours. Improved portions of WYO 530 have wider shoulders and additional passing lanes, though they usually remain two lanes wide.

Much of the eastern road’s alignment was built during the 1970s. Officials in Utah and Wyoming had planned a single numbered route between Moab and Yellowstone; in 1981, AASHTO recommended extending US 191 over roads including WYO 373 to the Utah line. The old numbers were retired in 1982. By then, the Green River had become a reservoir behind the dam at Red Canyon, completed in 1964.

Begin in Green River, where Expedition Island’s park commemorates John Wesley Powell’s river expeditions. WYO 530 runs south along the western side of the Green River and reservoir to the Utah line. On the eastern leg, US 191 heads north from Minnie’s Gap through 51 miles of rugged desert country to I-80 west of Rock Springs.

moments.title: Green River
moments.text: Water helped decide which town would keep the railroad. When Union Pacific reached Green River in 1868, its officials found an established town and moved their planned division point 12 miles west to Bryan on Blacks Fork. Then drought dried up Blacks Fork, forcing the railroad back to Green River for locomotive water; Bryan became a ghost town. The surviving original downtown core now forms a historic district that includes the Union Pacific depot. The current depot was completed in 1910. A lookout known as a crow’s nest was added to its trackside roof during the 1940s.

moments.title: Expedition Island
moments.text: A stone marker in Expedition Island’s public park commemorates John Wesley Powell’s river journeys. His 1871 expedition started here; the park is also believed to mark the departure point of his 1869 journey down the Green and Colorado rivers. River erosion divided the original island in two. The southern island contains the park, with a recreation center and a tree-fringed grassy area. A road bridge connects it to the north bank, and a pedestrian bridge reaches it from the south. Expedition Island received National Historic Landmark designation in 1968 for its association with the expeditions and their departure point.
moments.notice: The park’s stone marker commemorates Powell’s expeditions.

moments.title: Flaming Gorge Reservoir
moments.text: Flaming Gorge Reservoir covers a narrow, steep-sided canyon whose rock includes sandstone and hard quartzite interspersed with softer layers. Construction of the dam began in 1958 and ended in 1964, impounding the Green River. Most of the reservoir lies in southwestern Wyoming, with part in northeastern Utah. Dutch John, Utah, was built as a construction base and then an administrative site. WYO 530 follows the western side of this water. The canyon’s softer layers include shale, siltstone and argillite. Near the dam, a road cut exposes a fault scarp on its southbound side.
